title: A pricing page for a community sports club
metaTitle: A club pricing page that shows fit
excerpt: A club fees page should show what the price includes, what it leaves out, and a path to membership or the schedule. Publish the shape of the fee.
alt: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table. The laptop is where a fee has to become understandable.
caption: A person in a purple shirt types on a bright blue laptop at a round table. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a club fees page show first?
faqs.answer: Show the offer the fee belongs to, the number, and the period, then what is included and what is not. A new member is judging fit, which means whether this fee buys the week they imagined. A paragraph about community above a hidden number spends the opening on the wrong fact.

faqs.question: Should a standard membership require a quote?
faqs.answer: A standard fee is a published fact. Put the number, the period, and the boundary on the page. Quotes fit custom work. They turn an ordinary joining decision into correspondence the club will answer late.

faqs.question: How should trials and concessions be written?
faqs.answer: Give the trial its own line: whether it is free, whether the fee is credited if they join, and who must stay with a junior. State concessions as rules you will actually apply, such as a household cap. Leave off a discount the treasurer will refuse at the desk.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing Title Links in Google Search

markdown:
A community sports club pricing page is where a possible member judges fit. Show what the fee includes, what it leaves out, and a way to see membership or the schedule. Put the shape of the price on the page. People ask anyway, and a hidden number reads as a trick.

The page is a comparison they run in their head: this club against a gym, a casual game, or another club across town. Give them the facts that comparison needs. Spare them a scavenger hunt.

## Fit is the decision the fee is serving

A person deciding whether to join already has a rough budget. They are trying to learn whether this fee buys the week they imagined. A social player wants to know they can come twice and skip a month without a lecture. A parent wants to know the junior fee covers coaching, and whether match fees arrive later as a surprise. A competitive athlete wants to know whether the fee is the training, or only the right to be selected.

Write the page for those questions. Lead with the offer each fee belongs to, then the number, then the boundary. A table with three columns and no sentences forces the reader to invent the meaning of "full membership." They will invent it wrong, then feel misled at the desk.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on [how long people stay](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) still applies on a fees page. Users often leave in 10 to 20 seconds unless the value is clear within about 10. A pricing page that opens with a paragraph about community, and parks the numbers in a download, spends that window on mood. The number is the value on this page. Show it.

The same research notes that people read only about a quarter of the text on a page they visit. So the included list has to be short enough to finish. Five true lines beat fifteen lines that repeat "access to our community."

## What the fee includes

Name the sessions, the people, and the practical things the money covers. Coached training on two weeknights. A nominated social session. League entry for the senior squad. A club shirt for juniors, if that is true. Facility hire, so they are paying for the hall. Insurance, if the membership includes it and you can say so accurately.

Be specific about time. "Unlimited classes" means something only if the timetable can absorb a new person. If the popular session is capped, say the fee includes the right to book, subject to space. A promise the schedule cannot keep becomes a complaint in week three.

If there are tiers, give each tier a job in the member's language. Social. Training. Competing. Family. Student. The labels should match how the club already talks at registration, not how a software template names plans. "Gold" and "Platinum" tell a sports club member nothing about Tuesday.

Put the billing period in the same line as the price. Per season, per term, per month, per visit. A season fee and a monthly fee are different shapes. Showing both without saying which one a new person is expected to choose creates a fake choice. Recommend the path a typical new member takes, and let the other prices sit beside it as alternatives with reasons.

## What the fee does not include

The boundary is what makes the price believable. Match fees. Travel to away games. Kit beyond the shirt. Court hire if someone wants an extra hour. Tournament entry. A gun, a boat, a stick, or a pair of shoes the club does not lend. Say these in a short list under the price, in the same visual style as the included list, so they are part of the offer and easy to scan.

Parents in particular look for the second bill. If the headline junior fee excludes a compulsory kit pack and a registration levied by the association, print those amounts or the range. "Additional costs may apply" is the sentence that sends a careful parent to another club that was willing to be plain.

Trials deserve their own line. Free first session. A paid trial week. A trial that requires a parent to stay. If the trial fee is credited against membership when they join, say that. It changes the risk of showing up once.

Concessions belong here too, stated as rules rather than as a vibe. Students with an ID. A household cap. A volunteer discount with the hours attached. If the club cannot administer a discount, leave it off the page. A price the treasurer will refuse at the table is worse than a single public rate.

## Show the shape, then the schedule

Do not make people ask for the shape of the price. The shape is the number, the period, what is inside, and what is outside. A form that says "request a quote" is the wrong tool for a standard membership. Quotes fit custom work. A club's ordinary fee is a published fact.

Some clubs hesitate because a rival might undercut them, or because a committee has not agreed. The rival already knows, if anyone local cares. The committee's disagreement is a reason to decide, and it is a poor reason to publish a blank. If the fee is under review, say the current fee and the date it applies. An honest current number beats a page that pretends the club is bespoke.

Once the shape is visible, offer the way forward: see membership or the schedule. The price answers "can I see myself paying this." The schedule answers "can I actually attend." A fees page that never links the timetable strands the person who is ready. Use the same words as the homepage button, so the path feels like one site.

If registration is a form, put the form after the facts, on the same page or one click away. Ask for the name, the session they want, a contact, and anything safety requires. Collect medical detail at the moment it is needed, with a reason printed beside the field. Ten fields before they have seen the timetable is how a ready member gives up.

## Ages, squads, and the fee that changes

One club often sells several products under one word, membership. Separate them when the price or the promise changes. Juniors. Youth. Seniors. A development squad with limited places. A casual punch-card for people who travel for work.

Each block can be short. Who it is for. The fee and the period. Three included items. Two excluded items. The link to that part of the schedule. Repeating that pattern is a kindness. It lets a parent skip the senior block without feeling they missed a caveat in the prose.

If a squad has selection, say so next to the fee. Paying does not equal a match-day place, if that is the rule. People can accept a hard rule. They resent discovering it after they have transferred the money. Write the rule in one sentence, in the same size as the price, so it is part of the contract they can see.

Family fees need an example. Two adults and one junior, with the arithmetic done once on the page, so nobody has to build a spreadsheet to know the household. One worked example is enough. A second example helps only if the rule is odd, such as a cap after the third child.

## Keep the page current, and readable

Put a date on the fees. "Fees for the 2026 season" is a title a treasurer can update without redesigning the site. Google's guidance on [title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) warns that an obsolete title, such as a year that no longer matches the visible heading, is one reason a search result title gets replaced. A fees page with last year's year in the title and this year's numbers in the table is that mistake in a club's voice. Update both.

The visible heading should match the title. One clear heading: the fees, and the season they cover. Secondary headings can name social, junior, and competing. They should look like sections, so the main title stays the fees.

When the committee changes a number, change the page the same day. A screenshot in a group chat will outrun a stale site, and then the site looks careless. If a studio built the page, the club should be able to edit the numbers without a new project. That is a reasonable thing to ask for in the build: the fees as content, the layout as something that survives an edit.

Avoid a PDF as the only source. A PDF is easy for the treasurer and clumsy on a phone. If you need a PDF for the noticeboard, generate it from the same facts. Two sources of a fee will diverge by November.

## From the fee to the offer behind it

A clear fees page assumes the club can say what people are buying. If the offers themselves are still a list of vague program names, fix that next. Each offer needs an outcome, a boundary, and the step that follows, which is still to see membership or the schedule. That is the work of [the services page a community sports club actually needs](/blog/the-services-page-a-community-sports-club-actually-needs).

If you want a second pair of eyes on the order of these pages before you design them, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the current fee sheet, including the costs you usually explain only when someone asks.
